blocks.x: Yeah, on a New Year's Eve night, playing for this big lumberman up in Kansas, the only girl for pleasure, yeah, I'll go play. They had to hire six men for New Year's Eve, that was the union's law. I wouldn't have got in on that job, because he hadn't made a contract before, the union said they had to have six. So they got me on bass and another fellow on guitar, some Italian fellow. They went there and the job paid thirty dollars. Each hour overtime was ten dollars an hour, we would pay three hours overtime. That was the last job, we paid sixty dollars on the union's Eve night. Last job we played, huh? Yeah, he had venison sausage made out of dim eating. Oh man, that big guy had everything you could imagine. That was really the last job that I had played. I had a job one time with him over at Ackerman, you know, he was the president of this here Oak, of the Colton Cornwall Club, and here they are. Cap, he had a reception there, he hired Tony Capone with four pieces. Me, Tony Capone, a guitar player and Charlie Fishbein. Well the guitar player never did show up. Now you know what the rhythm I had, the bass in them. I had that, I had that, that happened to me on Mardi Gras Day. Yeah, I had a rhythm on the bass in them, and they never had a talk of them one time. That happened to me on one of those stands on Canal Street Mardi Gras Day, the little Chink Martin Jr. didn't show up. Bass? No, on guitar. On guitar. We had a bass, we had Sherwood Manjapani on bass. Yeah, he did. And little Chink Martin was supposed to come on guitar, and he came whimpering around, I couldn't get a hold of a guitar, Johnny. Couldn't get a hold of a guitar. Boy, I let out at him, I'm telling you. I sure let him know what I thought about. This day when they shut up one. They don't care a thing about what they do, you know. I mean ruin your whole band for the whole day. They had to struggle up there for what, six hours? I don't know what it was, but struggling up there without any harmony at all, except from the bass fiddle. You like that? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Three front lines and a bass fiddle. Four pieces, you see. Boy, that's a lot of fun to have to struggle through that for six hours. The rhythm is out, you just got a bass fiddle in and whoop where you have to. You got a little harmony, you know, so you can attach yourself to that harmony all right, but I mean after all there's not enough harmony in the bass fiddle. But this, I asked Tony, I said, what happened to the day I was just getting there? I said, he think it was tomorrow night. Remember how I used to do them guys in the spot jobs? Used to make a mistake, I had a little notebook, a slip of paper, and make a job. I had a band one time, Johnny, before you played with me. I was in such a demand, people used to ring me up what date you got up so we can give a dance. I'm not kidding you. That's true. You used to have a whole bunch of bands. That's true, they used to ring me up what date you got up when you were dancing. This guy had all the music tied up in the audience. That's right. I had the boys of Bahamians, had Hermes, and I was the first band playing Hermes, I still got to one of the seven years in there yet. All the different carnival balls. Those were the balls, did you do much of the parade work too? Oh that parade work. Oh did he? Yeah. Boy I was right up in the head. He had everything, he had a whole bunch of bands out. I had one of the best marching bands in the city, for the ten men. The men in my lineup was this, Harry Shannon, you didn't know him. Oh. You know Leon Danena. Yeah. He played trumpet. Harry Shannon. Danena played trumpet. He was a piano player and one of the best bass players in town, did you know that? The piano man? I'm talking about the- The fellow that's directing the police band today. Danena used to be at Four Chain High School? He's got the police band- He's a trumpet player? Well I said he played with me. Oh God I say. I'll tell you. He played trumpet with me, he played string bass with me, he played piano, you ask him. Every time I meet them, you know what he does to me? What? He was a player, he was playing a dedication with the police band. I left there looking and he was getting ready to start the bass. I left the whole way. Who else did you have in your marching band? I had a little, uh, Melon Bonina, Georgia Board, and, uh, Harry Shannon, who was my three trumpets. I had a fellow named Johnny Getty playing alto horn, a peck horn, and one peck horn. I had a fellow named Bob. Fred Dan Tagner playing alto saxophone, Georgia played- Who was on alto saxophone? Fred Dan Tagner. Oh. He used to play with Buckethead. Oh I know, yeah. He used to play with us in Texas. Oh man, powerful. Yeah. He was powerful. Wonderful attack. And then, when George was playing center saxophone, this was supposed to be a brass band, man, they were heavy. And they had, uh, Eddie Iman from Pace, a suit of phone, he bought that suit of phone from Mackey. Lefty Iman. He bought that suit of phone from Mackey. Red Mackey. Red Mackey, yeah. He still got the same suit of phone yet, I believe. Well I had, uh, a fellow by the name of, playing bass drum, and had Frisco on snare drum, and this fellow playing bass drum, Spora. He was a good man. Not Spobora. And we used to play like- Not Tony Spargo, Spobora. No, Spora. Spora, Spora, Spora, yeah. He was an old time bass drum. Yeah. And, uh, we used to play with Heather Morrissey, he even got the Morrissey from the Shrine Band, on the card. Yeah. Tent Commanders, all that big moorers. You see us coming down that street there. We was coming around, we was coming around, making a turn into Canal Street, and Ralph Shabawa was the secretary of union. He looked up to me and said I thought they were claiming and then bang, all of us, you know how the boys, they'd sooner play music than each. They were, 90% of them weren't playing for money. It was just, just, just that place. I don't know what they were, but that was it. Man, they fucked proud. I said they had red ribbons on the end of my drum, and I was shaking. You all smoking? No thanks, I remember the insurance. Well, tell me I'm glad you come around. The doctor, the doctor still lets you smoke, huh boy? Man, I smoke a cotton cell the rest of the week. I don't go food to no doctors, they're waiting them guys, you better off. My wife just went through that hospital clinic jail, and they fell around and busted their head wide open, and I brought her up there in the morning and said, that wasn't the cause of the cause of the cause of the give me Debbie, the one right there. Went through all those tests, and he gave her some little beef pills. She had a blood clot on the opposite side of the head. Oh, really? Yeah. That's fine. You have to watch that. It's a good thing he went there. You're going to go to the doctors and not me. When I, one time I had a play, I had four places over, over, over, over. The county, you know, part one, solo one, part one, solo one, and one of them was a dog on one of them. I had to give them away. And I was cutting grass with an electric plumber. You know, I said, I got short ones. I shot an electric more on Sunday, that's the grass. Let the grass grow. That was it. That was it. When you grew up with the grass, I thought something was going to hurt me. Well, that's all right if you've got sense enough to do that, you see. But a lot of people keep on going. You know, after that they go rest up and then they go back to it. Well, you don't have to go to a doctor if you do that, because the doctor is going to tell you to do that. I've been running over the covers for 20 years. But I had a place at Military Road, I had a place at McCombs, I had a place, I had two places in Chinchube and one on the Madisonville Harbor was the last place I sold. And I had a couple pieces of ground. I sold and sold it all. I'm in money. I bought one a lot for $50 and sold it for $4.50. I bought one for $100 and sold it for $1,000. It was the last piece I sold. I thought the cars were going to come through and get a boom, boom, boom, boom. Well, everything did go up. But they said there wasn't much of it to sell it, nobody could sell it. I was talking to the old Dean of Deanna. You got it here? Yeah. You got it here? Back of the garage there. You don't want to get it? And each flat trombone. Each flat valve trombone. We used to play it with Jack Ray when I pushed out the plate and he used to be, oh, what are you going to do with this? Look at this. You know that? Oh. You know that? Oh, yes, I have one of those. You know? I hope I still have it. Is that your one? He sent me one once. Is that your old? Yes. That's my old. I haven't seen that. Well, ain't you in this picture, Mr. Russell? Oh, look at this. Chris Hackney Show. That's in 1925, huh, Hackney? Was that 25? No. No. No. I played violin. I know you ain't, but the Souchant is a... Yes, Souchant. Here's Souchant right here. And here's Earl Crom. Yeah, I remember that. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my old boy. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my old boy. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. I remember that. Yeah. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my name, all of the sort of stories. Mm-hmm. Yeah. I shoved them on the side. Let me go see if I can get them. Sure, I'll let the rest of them have been. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Tutula Akhenna's father. This is George's son. And here's Elrin Mazur, the fellow who played clarinet with me on that Victor record. You know, the ex- I've got this date on the tape there on here. It was September 28, 1952. And that's the... I have one. You sent me one. I'm hoping I didn't loan that to John Snyder and that he kept it. I haven't seen that for a few years. I must have it at home. I sure haven't seen it for a while. I know I have. Do you want to read it again, John? No, no. I got it at home. That's the old horn. Oh, look at that. I got it real short. I thought it would be any longer. Fifty-four years old. Now, is that how it isn't Ben? You had that fifty-four years. You had that fifty-four years. No, no. Is that the same kind of going on in 52? Is that the same pinch as an outdoor horn, Ben? I can eat that outdoor. I can eat that outdoor. I can eat that outdoor. I can eat that outdoor. I can eat that outdoor. I can eat that outdoor. Is that a silver horn? No. No. Gold brass. Gold brass. I want to show you to leave them. No. We should pass him up over here. Yeah, I see his pictures. Yeah, I see his pictures. Yeah. I can wear a lot of mouthpiece for a room. See, I'd like to see how I get a couple of notes on it. Huh? Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Well listen, that thing is hard to play that high pitch on. You don't like those high pitch on, do you? You like the B flat, don't you? Yeah, the B flat. The B flat's better. I can't wait to try it.
This show you were talking about, they advertised it as a jazz band, do you say?

No, I want to try to get it right. So, when we got off the train, we told the police we were waiting for Mike Pristler, so you ain't gonna catch Mike around here this time, they'd be seeing you fellas catch a cab. Go out to the El Sonny Cafe, the cab driver knows right where to go, so we went out there and George Pristler was there, he was in a colored polo.
I think you're playing see the third line, I mean the third space, and it sounds the first line. But George used to play an awful lot of picnics, didn't you?

Oh, yeah. Most of your work was picnics, wasn't it? In those days, New Orleans used to give a terrible lot of picnics, didn't they? That was all the rage for a time, wasn't it? Out at Nuremberg on a Sunday, if they didn't have 25 or 30 bands, they didn't have two. And out at West End, too? All over the places. West End, they had two places at West End. One of them was Brunnings, Pavilion. They have all their things. If they had a dollar and a half a couple to go there, and they give you a chicken and spaghetti dinner, and hot dog sandwiches and beer all day long for that dollar and a half a couple. Over the by, they call it, over the Rhine was Smith's Cottage. The only two places. Well, they was crowded every Sunday. Is that where Brunnings used to play, the Brunnings Brothers? Well, the Brunnings played all over different places, you see? That's what I want to tell you about when you ask about playing Color and White together. I had a job at Smith's Cottage one Sunday, and I wanted to get musicians together. I don't know what happened, but then I got a hold of Dave Pertons on valve trombone, Archie on clarinet, and Baptiste on quine on fiddle, and me, and Harry Shannon, and Rag Baby Stevens, three white brothers and three niggas. I don't know what happened. Well, that takes, let me see, that takes the glory away from Mesro, doesn't it? Yeah, Mesro. And everybody can dial it. You know Dave Pertons. There's a clarinet player from Chicago who brags about being the first white man to play with Negro musicians. So, uh... You tell me about Baptiste on quine, the fiddle player. Archie on parquet, the clarinet player. Dave Pertons is a valve trombone player, a B-flat valve trombone. It sounded like a baritone, you know, just big, big, big, big, big one, see? And he used to go boom, boom, boom, boom. Really going down again. Isn't he the one that... One time he used to call me, of course, the brothers were killed. They come to Happy Children's Black and White Band. That's right. But we used to play them, though, boy. We used to play them, boy. Isn't he the valve trombone player that ended up with Duke Ellington? No. He was from New Orleans. Sixth fella. Dave Pertons, you mean? Well, that one of those... That valve trombone player you named a minute ago. Color fella. Dave Pertons. He was a great, big man. Great, big fella. He had red skin. Uh-huh. He looked right into you.
Yeah, Papa Lane, though, he played with him, too.

Oh, yeah. He played with him, played with Lane before he would play with me. He used to teach music, too. That's right. He'd teach routine, they called it, by numbers. That's how he used to teach them. And he used to rent instruments. He had a room full of instruments. Like all these colored fellas. So much... You want to rent a drum board or rent a drum or rent a horn. He'd rent it to them. He used to make part of money like that, renting. He'd keep a list of them, check on them. They'd bring them back to church so much as they want. He'd be back. I went back at his house. First time I went back to see him, he's... I'm not going to do it with a color later. Come on. Mr. Dave Puggin's good. He said, yeah. He went to the home. He said, yeah, come on in. He said, all right. He'd come out. I said, I used to put your money. He said, I hired him for a job. And he was in the union, you see. The reason why they kept him in the union, he had the original chart in his pocket. They couldn't throw him out. They couldn't throw him out. He had a really short of another union. He was good, Happy? Huh? Was he good? You mean for playing jazz? Jazz, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He's one of the first. One of the best. He's one of the first. Dave Puggin, I feel back to each on quine, used to play alto horn in the bands. He's fiddled in the dance band. Listen, I hope you can answer this question because I sure would love to know what's... Did you ever hear Buddy Boland play? Yeah. Tell me what style he played. King Boland was... Did he play like Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong? All of them played pretty in the same style. Louis Armstrong was a little bit different because Louis Armstrong was... He got the wine, you know. Louis Armstrong didn't get by what he's playing. He's got the rival voice he had. You know what I mean? But I saw King Oliver when he was working down in the story building. King Oliver. Right in the corner, we used to stand outside and listen to him playing. He never used a mutiny horn. He had an extra mouthpiece, you see? See like this mouthpiece? Put that mouthpiece on. That's what he used to use, it's a mutiny. He used to use a piece of pint too, didn't he? Yeah. A piece of pipe, so did Buddy Boland, I believe. That's right, him and... A piece of... A piece of gas pipe. One pop it off the other one. Man, he used to get a... Ooh, boy. How... Man, you could hear him on Canal Street. Well, would you say that Buddy Boland played sort of like Joe Oliver? Practically like that. Now, that's... I'm awful glad to get that played. Buddy Boland and King Oliver was... There was a metaphor that had a band of colors for the... Oh, good man. Spread... Pickle up. Bad Frank? Bad Frank. Bad Frank. Bad Frank. He had a band. He used to get around and get in our way now and then try to knuckle in on down. He had a good outfit too. Yeah. Yeah, but he used to lead his band with his pickle up. I know Joe Oliver had a good outfit because I used to dance to his band. He was wonderful. We had a fellow in the old days when we'd go around and give kids nickels. He called him King, King Watsky, the fiddle player. Remember him? You remember him? That's all way back. King Watsky was the fiddle player. Well, listen now... Go around and get kids nickels and call him King Watsky. So he'd get that nickname King Watsky. So all these things, King Oliver and King Boland. He wanted to be king too because he lived back amongst those niggas back on for extra. See? What kind of a band did Buddy Boland have? Did he have a good band? Yeah, a regular seven, eight piece band. I mean, did he have outstanding players in it? One of the best of them. I don't know. I know Robichaux. You remember Robichaux? Oh, well, yeah. George Bakke. I shoot Bakke the clarinet player that played with us. He's brother used to play clarinet with Robichaux. Well, Robichaux had a straight band. That's right. Strictly legit. No blood. No, Strictly legit. That's what we used to call that then day. It was tiresome. They used to play out at the Yacht Club and I used to hate to go out there because of that reason. Well, they had a few good players in it, you see, but I mean, he kept them straight laced. He wanted to be a gentleman, you know. Yeah. He was a very light colored fellow. Yeah. And he was dignified looking, you remember? That's right. He was a good musician. He was raised a gentleman, you know. He was a good musician. He had a very good education and all that. And he didn't want to be a low class Negro. He wanted to be a gentleman. He was a good guy. And he kept his band straight and that's what ruined his band. But he had all the top white. Yeah. He used to play at the Louisiana, you remember? And he used to play at the Yacht Club and the Boston Club and places like that. He used to play a lot of society white. Yeah. Who was this other colored fellow, crippled fellow? Oh, P. Ron. P. Ron. Yeah. P. Ron. Thought he was, he wouldn't mix with the white people too much and that's what ruined him. He was at the Yacht Club and a fellow by the name of, was a steward out there running the hell away from there. And I got, did you play with me at the Yacht Club? Well, not, I played spot jobs at the Yacht Club. No, I had a job study job. I'll tell you how I had it. No, I didn't play that study. The last big American Legion meeting here, convention, was at the Yacht Club. Where they split up. Lannis, the ball, big ball czar, he come down at the time. And I'll never forget, when I went to the Yacht Club, I had to play spot work lined up. And a fellow by the name of, he was steward, he wanted me to come take the job at the Yacht Club. I said, well I can't take the job. I said, because you want me on Saturday and Sunday nights maybe? I said, during the week I'll, I'll take a look at what I do with you, Sheila. I said, anybody that hires the club, rents the club, got to rent the club, including the band, no matter what it is. And that was on my contract. And I played there a whole year. No matter what come into the club, I was there. Man, he did a penis and everything, man, stuffed lobsters and all kinds of stuff in there. And we played there a whole year for them. Well anyhow, he had left there, and he took that job at the New Country Club. New Orleans Country Club? Not the New Orleans Country Club, the other club. Oh, the Jewish Country Club. Yeah, he left, he went over there. And he wanted us to come over there. But I played two jobs in there, because he couldn't give me the right contract that I wanted, you see. I played two jobs. But I finished my job at the, at the, at the, at the Yacht Club. And we played there. And no matter what came in, they had this big American League convention. And they had a banquet out there. They took up the whole floor, not even a dance space, nothing, all tables. And there was the band. The band was there trying to play. But this fellow ladders, he wanted to dance. And he started shoving the dog on the table. But I don't think that's the dance. That's been a long time. He was a young, a fellow young, a fellow young. He wanted to dance, just started to dance. First thing that had all the tables piled up on top and went and started to dance after it got done eating. But there was a certain time he had a light. You know, where he was sitting at his desk. When to, when to, when to play and when to stop. And you put that light on, you stop. Don't play as long as you see that light playing. Oh, it's because it was serving, you see. And when it got through serving, put the light on, then we start to play for him to dance. That's how he was singing for God. I had, I had, uh. Johnny Biesoffer must have been playing trumpet with you then. That's right. Johnny Biesoffer was playing trumpet with me. Charlie Hardman played trombone with you? Oh, I played trombone. Oh, you did? I played trombone. And, uh, Lefty Ironman. How does Lefty Ironman spell his last name? E-I-E-R-N-A-N. E-I-E-R-N-A-N. E-I-E-R-N-A-N. Eddie Ironman. He lives over in Greffman. I was born a place in Greffman. Oh, yeah? He lives over in Greffman. I wasn't explaining anyone out at all. And who else was in your band at that time, George? Was your son on clarinet? No, I had a fellow by the name of, yeah, George and works. And I had a fellow by the name of Dixon playing piano. Do you know Willie Dixon, the piano man? He was very good. Very good man. But he left me at, and we left the yard club, and they took a job at, uh, on St. Charles Street, where they have a, where they're going over St. Charles, they go in one way, they had two places. They're going to Common, where the old, uh, what was the name of that place? I don't know what it was called around, it was an old German Colorado. Lehigh, Dixon, the Ratsgiller. The Ratsgiller? The Ratsgiller. No, it wasn't the Ratsgiller, no. Across from the St. Charles Theater? Yeah, St. Charles Hotel. On Common Street, they come in one way, they had a place, then they go around, and you come to another place, and they go around, and you come to another place, and say, oh, St. Charles. I can't think of the name of it all, but that's where he worked piano. Not Cobbs, huh? He worked in the back, and he'd entertain for both places, you see? Oh, really? It kind of doubled him up. It wasn't Cobbs, huh? Uh-uh. We worked Cobbs upstairs a couple of times, too. Johnny Deidre had that job. Yeah. That's why he broke in Benny Darden on trombone. He took Benny Darden and played trombone. He couldn't always know it. Johnny Perrani used to play there, too. I believe he played there with Johnny Deidre, didn't he? He may have, I don't remember that. I don't remember that outfit, what he had, but I know that he took in Benny Darden, and Benny Darden couldn't play trombone. Who? But Johnny Deidre broke him in, made a trombone, put a trombone man out of him. He played a long time. He wrote a little trombone. He had three brothers play music. Charlie Darden, Benny Darden. Benny Darden. Benny Darden. He was that a clown and a... Charlie Darden played... Fiddle. Fiddle and trumpet. Well, what Darden is that played trumpet? Him? Charlie Darden played trumpet and fiddle. That's the one that shakes hands with you and crushes your hand all the time. No, that's Benny, the big, very big heavy fella. Yeah. Charlie's dead, he died. Yeah. I don't know whether Benny's living or not, the other fellow, the other clown that played, he died. The fellow that crushes your hand is still living, because I was talking to him a few months ago. He owns a lot of property and he's retired and he's sorry he's retired. Yeah. Yeah, it's eating on him, you know. He don't have anything to do. You know what happened that his daddy had the contract with the New Orleans Public Service to go around pumping the water out of these gas mains, you know, and go around with these couple pumps. But his daddy was living on Florida Street and they used to, all the boys, they tied up and they used to pump and go from one different place to pump out water. That's where he made his money. And after the old man died, he had his fuzz, then Benny, Benny took it up to the Trump World Play. He was the one, the last one I heard, anyway he made all this money here in the country. He was the one going around with us. And it got so, so that they used to change that, but he's a big man, now that he used a gasoline pump.
Well, I was going to ask you a little bit more about Papa Jack Lane's band, his dance band. They weren't legitimate sounding. How did they sound? How were they? Very good. Very good.

One man, the Pembert of Born here, to hear what he was going to do, to catch it. If you didn't have any good air with Jack Lane, you wouldn't know a musician. Air comes with him and everything. You had to be what they call fake musician. And it was strictly jazz, wasn't it? Strictly.
Fake musician. No, there wasn't any legitimate sound like the Robichoke band. No, no, no. Nothing like that.

He had this town tied up one time, Jack Lane. Man, everything was the Reliance band and from there on that was it. I remember when I was a young fellow, before I started to play music, he used to play, you fool around with the guitars and stuff like that. We used to go around with Christian, you know what I'm saying? Christian the fiddle player, his daddy. He was a good trumpet man too, this fiddle player. His daddy had two street bands, each one of his sons run the band. Well, he had everything tied up. It was all brass work that time. Strictly, strictly legit, you know what I mean? Yeah. Brass bands playing all these balls around. The old Fifteen Hall and Seven magazine had blown down that time. He did every Saturday night with a band. He beat on the yard first. Maybe the Washington Terrier would have one. And they advertised Christian's band. Christian's band here, Christian's band here. Everybody knew where the old man would be on one. Was he a male Christian's daddy? No relation at all, but they spoke their names the same. No relation. That was a brass band. All brass.
They played dances.
Brass band, dances.
But they'd swing then, too, didn't they? Well, they played good dance music.

Them days used us to play a lot of viola, the lances, charlages and square dances. I never forget when we'd go to a fall when I was caught with my wife. They'd have lances, you know, they'd dance. They'd dance, they'd dance, they'd dance. They'd bump and stop. Then they'd have to go make up the sets. They'd have to stop. Wait a minute, the fellas on the floor come in and holler. They had badges on, you know, holler. Wait hold up, I got another one. I got another cup for this set. Another cup for this set. Another cup for this set. Then they'd go ahead and start. Then the people would dance on the set. While all the sets were dancing with the lances, you know, the square dances. They'd dance on the side of them, you see. Then they'd come in and keep on shoving us back to keep out of the way. Funny them, they. Then after that, they'd start this, used to call the bands ragtime. That's where Jack Lane and all of them started to call us a ragtime band. You want to know where the originate is, the name of jazz? No, I'd like to hear where.
You think they're named from New Orleans? I don't know. I've heard all different stories, but I never did know. That's right.

The original Dixieland jazz band, he can vouch for it is Nick LaRocca on, Jack and Abbey. He don't like to talk to nobody about nothing the way I understand. They went up there and they had a dance called a shimmy. And dancing around the Shilla Cafe, they used to call it ass dance, jazz. They called it jazz dance. And they called it first J-A-Z, then J-A-S, then J-A-S, then J-A-S, then J-A-Z. And they were the name originally. Harry James could tell you that today if he's living, I believe it's down in the French Quarter somewhere. They were the original, right there, jazz. And they called them a jazz band.
From the Chicago movement? That's right. That's right.

Right there. And the other thing was jaffy. We didn't know what jazz was down here. We went there. We called ourselves a ragtime band. To the rock around there, they called them the Nick LaRocca and jazz band. But before they first worked, there was the Dixieland band. They added the name jazz to it. They worked at the Shilla Cafe at a while. Of course you knew, some guy in New York made them a big oven and went to the Palais Royal.
